opus-5.5.text:
I think the key right now is honesty about where we actually are, and building the industry on real capability rather than on demos.

There's a lot of excitement about humanoid robots: robots dancing, doing backflips, performing at galas. Those things show real progress in hardware and motion control, and I don't want to dismiss them. But we have to be clear-eyed. A backflip is mostly a locomotion and control problem that can be solved in simulation and trained very well. What really matters for robots to enter factories, stores, and eventually homes is manipulation, the ability to generalize. Can the robot pick up an object it has never seen before, in a scene it has never been in, under lighting it wasn't trained on, and do it reliably, thousands of times a day? That's a much harder problem, and it's where the real value is.

So for healthy development, I'd emphasize a few things.

First, the data problem. Language models had the whole internet. Robots don't. Collecting real-world teleoperation data is expensive and slow, and it doesn't scale the way people sometimes imagine. That's why I believe strongly in synthetic data and simulation as the foundation, with real-world data used to align and fine-tune. If the industry's whole strategy is "hire more people to teleoperate," I don't think that leads to generalization at a reasonable cost.

Second, we need to find real commercial scenarios early, even if they're narrow. A robot that reliably does one valuable job, like retrieving goods in a pharmacy or handling parts on a production line, creates a closed loop. It earns money, it generates data from real deployment, and that data improves the model. This is much healthier than waiting for a perfect general-purpose household robot that may still be years away.

Third, not over-promising. If companies keep telling the public that every family will have a robot butler next year, then when that doesn't happen there's a backlash. Capital pulls back, and good teams get hurt along with the hype. I'd rather the industry say plainly: here's what we can do today, here's what we'll do in three years, and here's what's still a research problem.

And finally, I think the form factor should serve the task. "Humanoid" shouldn't be a religion. Sometimes wheels are better than legs; sometimes two arms on a mobile base gets you ninety percent of the value at a fraction of the cost and risk. The goal is embodied intelligence that's actually useful. The humanoid shape is a means, not the end.

So in short: real generalization, scalable data, genuine use cases, and honest expectations. If we get those right, I'm very optimistic about the long term.

r001.rationale: The response supports narrow, valuable commercial jobs that generate deployment data, but does not say a limited-functionality robot can be sold for further development.

r002.rationale: It recommends finding narrow commercial uses and describes a robot earning money, but does not identify delivering productivity as a product as the key to healthy development.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key is to resist the temptation to put on a show. Right now the whole industry is a little bit intoxicated. Every week there's a new demo video — a robot doing a backflip, a robot dancing, a robot pouring coffee — and the public, and frankly a lot of investors, are starting to believe that general-purpose humanoids are right around the corner. I don't think that's healthy, because the gap between a demo and a product is enormous, and when expectations run that far ahead of reality, you eventually get a correction that hurts everyone, including the teams doing serious work.

So the first thing I'd say is: be honest about where we actually are. The hardware has made real progress. Motors, actuators, the whole body — a humanoid can walk, can balance, can do some pretty impressive locomotion. But locomotion is not where the value is. The value is in the hands, in manipulation, in being able to go into an environment the robot has never seen before and do something useful with objects it has never touched before. And that part — the "brain," the generalizable embodied intelligence — is still very immature. We're nowhere near the equivalent of GPT-3 for robotics. Anyone who tells you otherwise is either confused or selling something.

The second thing is data. Large language models got to where they are because the internet handed them trillions of tokens for free. Robots have no internet to crawl. Every piece of interaction data has to be generated — through teleoperation, through simulation, through real-world deployment. And teleoperation alone doesn't scale; you can't have a human behind every robot forever. So I think the healthy path is for the field to take data seriously as a scientific problem, not just a labor problem. How do we combine simulation, synthetic data, and real-world data so the model actually generalizes? That's the crux, and I'd much rather see companies competing on that than on who has the flashiest video.

Third — and this is maybe a bit unpopular — I think we should stop insisting on the full humanoid form for every application. If the goal is to get real deployments and real data loops going, then put a dexterous hand and a good perception system on a wheeled base or a fixed arm, put it in a factory or a warehouse where it can actually do a task, and let it start accumulating experience. Legs are expensive, they introduce safety and reliability issues, and in most indoor commercial scenarios you don't need them yet. The humanoid shape is the long-term destination because the world is built for humans, but we don't have to buy the whole ticket on day one.

And the last point is about the ecosystem. Right now a lot of the capability is locked up inside individual companies, each building their own full stack from scratch. That's incredibly wasteful. Healthy development, to me, looks like some degree of open foundation models for embodied intelligence, shared benchmarks that actually test generalization rather than cherry-picked tasks, and a division of labor where not every startup has to reinvent the motor controller. If we can get to a point where the hardware is somewhat standardized and the intelligence layer can be shared and improved collectively, then the whole industry moves faster and the hype problem takes care of itself, because progress will be measurable instead of theatrical.

So — humility about the current state, real investment in the data problem, pragmatism about form factor, and more openness in the ecosystem. If we get those four right, I'm actually very optimistic. The ceiling here is enormous. I just want us to climb toward it instead of jumping and hoping.

astra-6.text:
I think the key at this stage is to connect technological progress with real needs. A humanoid robot can look impressive in a demonstration, but can it perform a useful task reliably, safely, and at a cost someone is willing to pay? That’s the test we need to focus on.

We should start with clearly defined applications, put robots to work in those settings, and use what we learn to improve them. That creates a productive cycle between deployment and development. We also need to be honest about what the technology can and cannot do. Ambition is important, but healthy development depends on steady improvements and realistic expectations.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that a robot with limited functionality can still be a product when sold for further development.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes useful tasks, deployment, and real needs, but does not identify delivering productivity as a product as the key.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to stay grounded in real needs. A humanoid robot can look impressive in a demonstration, but the more important question is whether it can reliably perform useful tasks, safely and at a reasonable cost.

At this stage, we need to spend more time testing robots in real environments, understanding where they fail, and using those failures to improve them. We also need to be clear about what still requires human assistance. That helps customers make informed decisions and gives developers meaningful feedback.

Healthy development means allowing room for long-term research while building a practical feedback loop: find a genuine need, test the technology, measure the results, and keep improving.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing, failure, and human assistance, but does not say that a robot with limited functionality can be sold as a product for further development.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes meeting real needs and performing useful tasks, but does not identify delivering productivity as a product as the key to healthy development.
